page: Vultr voc-c-2c-4gb-75s-amd is an entry-tier instance in the Optimized Cloud Compute family, configured with 2 dedicated vCPUs derived from 1 physical AMD EPYC core running at 2.0 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. Hardware features include 32 KB L1d cache, 512 KB L2 cache, and 16 MB L3 cache, along with support for AVX, AES-NI, and SHA-NI instruction sets. The server is allocated 4.0 GB of system memory, matching a 1:2 compute-optimized ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU, and includes a bundled 75 GB local NVMe SSD without discrete GPU accelerators. Networking provisions include one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Benchmark results demonstrate strong single-core compute performance, with stress-ng recording 2,929.97, placing it in the top 25% of tested systems. Geekbench single-core performance reached 1,817.0, supported by average throughput across gzip compression (27.69 GB/sec) and bzip3 decompression (11.33 GB/sec). However, multi-core capacity is constrained by the two-thread limit, as evidenced by a Geekbench multi-core score of 3,297.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 4,823.64, both positioning in the lower quartile. Memory throughput reflects average write speeds of 34.24 GB/sec for uncached blocks, but drops to weaker percentiles in read operations.

The presence of dedicated AMD CPU cores ensures consistent processing cycles compared to burstable or shared alternatives, though aggregate throughput remains bounded by core count. Results for database operations (PassMark score of 935.72) and static web serving throughput (2.39 GB/sec) place the instance in the bottom 10%, indicating that high-concurrency input/output tasks are bottlenecked by memory density and core parallelism. Redis SET throughput achieved 3.82 million operations per second, while small-model LLM text generation achieved an average 87.92 tokens per second.

Given its hardware baseline, the voc-c-2c-4gb-75s-amd is technically aligned with lightweight compute tasks requiring consistent single-threaded execution rather than high concurrency. It serves low-traffic microservices, administrative automation agents, small build workers, and background task handlers where dedicated execution is preferred over burstable capacity.
